## Project Context

The Late Middle Pleistocene (hereafter referred to as the "Chibanian") spans from approximatly 350 Ka to 100 ka 
and is characterized by `climate instability`, `shifting sea
levels`, and `faunal dispersals which reflect much of today's
modern biota`. As it pertains to paleoanthropology, the Chibanian hosts a minimum of three widely agreed 
upon hominin species: *Homo erectus* (~1.8 Ma-125 Ka), *Homo 
neanderthalensis* (~440 ka-30 Ka), and *Homo sapiens* (~300 
Ka-present). In addition to these agreed upon taxa, many scholars 
recognize or argue for the existence of additional hominin species 
designations. These include commonly discussed nomina such as *Homo 
heidelbergensis* and *Homo floresiensis*, as well as lesser understood taxa such as *Homo naledi*, *Homo longi*, and *Homo juluensis* (see Table 1). Further, while *Homo 
heidelbergensis* is a commonly referenced taxon, recent 
considerations have divided the assemblage into the already 
well-regarded *H. neanderthalensis* taxon throughout Europe and a 
new designation of *H. bodoensis* in Africa. The latter designation would also encapsulate the contended *H. rhodesiensis* named by Woodward in 1921.

| *H. floresiensis*      | ~100-50ka           | S.E. Asia/Indonesia  |
| *`H. heidelbergensis*`*| ~600-200ka          | W. Eurasia (see below)|
| *`H. naledi*`*         | ~335-236ka          | South Africa         |
| *`H. rhodesiensis*`*   |        N/A[^1]      | Zimbabwe             |
| *`H. bodoensis`*       |        N/A[^2]      | Africa/W. Eurasia    |
| *`H. longi`*           | ~309-138ka          | China                |

[^1]: *H. rhodesiensis* would have ICZN priority for the Kabwe/Broken Hill specimen if were to be removed from the *H. heidelbergensis* designation. Roksandic et al. 2022 challenge this designation on ethical grounds given the nomina's association with Cecil Rhodes and a call to remove taxonomic names with ethical baggage (i.e., racism, colonialism, genocide, and etcetera). 

[^2]: *H. bodoensis* is the taxonomic designation offered to replace *H. rhodesiensis* an encapsulate specimens such as Bodo, Kabwe, and others. There is no current precedent for such replacement by the current ICZN standards. As such, the ICZN will need to change the rules governing taxonomic designation before this taxon will be accepted.

Kaifu and Athreya (2024) suggest that the "high level of craniodental variability" observable in the Asian Chibanian fossils has "defied efforts" to classify them along morphological grounds (4). While not directly approaching the subject of how many species are present in this assemblage or where the species boundaries should be drawn, they outline theoretical explanations for where the observed variation might have come from. To sidestep the question (and reasonably so because it doesn't matter for their discussion) they fall back on Howell's use of Paleodemes to reflect "local populations of fossil taxa that are inferred to have shared a closer gene pool than their geographically and temporally more distant relative populations" (4).
